## XVI. Would owning Congo liberate us all?

Let's invoke the delusion once more — imagine if Africa owned the DRC — would that alone free the continent?

I want to answer the arithmetic first and the ownership second, because the arithmetic is where I have to be disciplined and the ownership is where I have to stop being polite.

The arithmetic. The DRC's untapped mineral resources are routinely valued at $24 trillion — repeated by the US government, the Atlantic Council, the World Bank's orbit and every article ever written on the subject. It is also an extrapolation from known reserves that lacks robust empirical foundation; valuations swing with market conditions and extraction capacity, and conservative institutional assessments are far more hedged. And in-ground value is not money. Spread across fifty years and a hundred and ten million people, even the optimistic figure is transformative rather than continentally redemptive.

So: no, the DRC alone does not liberate 1.5 billion people. I will not inflate a number to win an argument I can win without it.

Now ownership — and here I withdraw the word I used earlier, because it was a lawyer's word and this is not a legal question.

I wrote that the DRC already owns the DRC. That is true in the sense that a UN seat is true, and false in every sense that pays a wage.

Ask the only question that matters: where does the $24 trillion circulate?

Not in Kinshasa. Not in Kolwezi. It leaves as ore. The country produces 70–80% of the world's cobalt and earns roughly a billion dollars from it, against a lithium-ion battery market exceeding sixty billion a year. Mining captures about 5% of the value chain; cell manufacture and pack assembly capture 40%. Less than 5% of Africa's critical minerals are refined on the continent at all. Chinese state enterprises and policy banks control roughly 80% of the DRC's cobalt output; China processes 74% of the world's cobalt and 90% of its rare earths.

So what, precisely, does Congolese "ownership" consist of? The right to hold the asset while somebody else sets its price, moves it, refines it, and books the margin. That is not ownership. That is custody. A man who holds the deed to a house he may not enter, rent out or sell at his own price does not own a house. He is being made to guard one.

And the guarding is expensive, which is the second half of the machinery and the part I shall name correctly.

The war is not an interruption of the extraction. It is a component of it.

I am not claiming every militia was manufactured in a foreign office. I am claiming something more durable: that a state permanently at war cannot regulate, cannot tax properly, cannot enforce a contract, cannot insist on a refinery, and cannot say no. Instability is not a bug in the extraction model. It is the operating condition under which the extraction model achieves its best prices.

Look at how it is currently financed and you can see the loop closing. M23's control of the coltan-rich Rubaya mine yields roughly $300,000 a month, with at least 150 tonnes of tantalum ore smuggled to Rwanda per UN experts. In gold-rich Ituri, militias earned at least $140 million in mineral revenues in 2024. Rwanda's mineral exports rose from $772 million in 2022 to $1.1 billion in 2023 — a figure analysts note exceeds what its own production could plausibly generate — with UN experts finding Rwandan minerals mixed with those from M23-held territory. Kigali denies direct involvement. Kinshasa's finance minister put the annual smuggling loss at close to a billion dollars. M23's 2025 capture of Goma and Bukavu displaced 700,000 people; over 7,000 were killed in the Goma assault alone.

Note carefully what this is. This is not primarily white men taking African minerals. This is an African state — one of the best-governed on the continent by conventional metrics — accused by UN experts of laundering the minerals of a neighbour through its own export figures. Fragmentation does not only invite external predation. It manufactures internal predation. There would be no smuggling economy in the Kivus if there were no line to smuggle across.

## And then diplomacy arrives — which is the guise

The parallel is exact, and worth drawing slowly. In the nineteenth century the Bible went ahead and the flag followed: one instrument prepared the ground, the other took the title, and the sequence was always presented as service. The instruments have been retired. The sequence has not.

Today the war goes ahead and the agreement follows. February 2025: the European Parliament voted to suspend the EU's raw materials memorandum with Rwanda over the military presence and traceability failures — while the 2024 Global Gateway agreement facilitating mineral trade was not formally revoked. March 2025: President Tshisekedi reportedly proposed to President Trump military assistance to end M23 in exchange for US access to cobalt, tantalum and lithium, framed as advancing America's technological edge. December 2025: the Washington Agreements for Peace and Prosperity — security guarantees and troop withdrawals traded for direct access to Congolese mineral wealth, with a deep-sea port and land for US military bases attached (again—I hope the irony isn't lost on you!).

Read it as a sentence and it is unmistakable. Peace was sold to the Congolese, and they paid for it in cobalt.

Not brokered by the African Union. Not resolved by any continental security architecture — because there isn't one, because Nkrumah's African High Command was voted down at Monrovia in 1961 and never revived. A bilateral transaction between a fragmented state and a superpower, conducted over seven thousand bodies in Goma, and announced as a peace initiative.

The word "aid" does similar work. When a country's security, its mineral licensing, its health budget and its humanitarian relief are all supplied by external actors flying a multilateral flag, the argument about whether this counts as colonisation becomes semantic. A state that cannot fund its own army, its own courts or its own clinics has already transferred sovereignty; the only remaining question is the identity of the recipient, and the answer is written on the side of the Land Cruiser (Hint—dreamy blue eyes!—Again—I hope the sarcasm isn't lost on you!).

## Blum, and why I will not lean on him

William Blum's America's Deadliest Export: Democracy argues that America's stated commitment to democracy promotion is cover for economic and strategic interest — that the secret of US foreign policy is that there is no secret, the objective being dominance by available means. He documents the National Endowment for Democracy, founded 1983, as Washington's foremost non-military regime-change instrument.

Blum is a polemicist. The book is advocacy, not dispassionate scholarship — reviewers call it a sustained tirade, and it should be read as argument. Serious scholars of democracy promotion — Michael McFaul, Christopher Coyne — contest both his framing and his conclusions, and there is substantial literature arguing that democracy promotion has mixed motives and mixed results rather than uniformly cynical ones.

But you do not need Blum's strongest claims to make the structural point, and the structural point survives every objection to him:

A fragmented continent presents fifty-five separate negotiating counterparties, each individually weak, each with leaders whose political survival can be influenced, and each holding resources external powers need. Whether or not any given intervention is cynically motivated, the opportunity structure for external leverage exists because of fragmentation, not despite it.

That is the sentence. It requires no villain. It survives good faith. It would be true if every foreign minister in the world were a saint.

So let me restate the point I was too careful to make the first time.

The constraint was never who holds the title. It is who holds the refinery, who sets the price, who writes the tariff schedule, who accredits the bar — and who is permitted to be at peace. Congo is not poor because it does not own its minerals. Congo is being kept in a condition in which ownership cannot be exercised.

Which is why a continental answer is not sentiment. One buyer's market and fifty-five sellers is a price. One seller's bloc and four buyers is a negotiation. The Congolese cannot fix this alone, and that is not a failure of Congolese character. It is the arithmetic of being made to stand alone.

## XVII. How a banana republic gets its name

I reached for this analogy early, and having looked properly at where the phrase comes from, I am not sure I have ever encountered a cleaner parable for what is being done to us.

The term was coined by the writer O. Henry in 1904, describing Honduras. But the machinery it names belongs to the United Fruit Company, and the full machinery looked like this: a foreign corporation acquires the land, then the railways, then the ports, then the telegraph. It sets wages. It selects the crop. It influences who governs. The country's economy becomes an extension of one company's logistics chain — and the people who live there become, functionally, tenants on ground their grandfathers walked freely.

Then Guatemala elected Jacobo Árbenz, and Guatemala tried to stop it.

Two per cent of the population held seventy-two per cent of the arable land, and only twelve per cent of private land was being used. United Fruit owned forty-two per cent of Guatemalan land and cultivated fifteen per cent of what it held. Árbenz's Decree 900 redistributed uncultivated land, compensating owners in bonds maturing over twenty-five years, valued according to the claims those owners had made on their own previous tax returns.

Stop there. That is the most elegant policy instrument I have ever read about.

We will pay you exactly what you told the tax office it was worth.

United Fruit had been serially undervaluing its holdings to avoid tax. Árbenz offered $1.2 million based on the company's own declared figures; United Fruit and the State Department demanded $16 million.

Secretary of State John Foster Dulles was a former lawyer for United Fruit. His brother Allen, director of the CIA, had sat on the company's board. In August 1953 Eisenhower authorised Operation PBSUCCESS — a $2.7 million covert programme to overthrow Árbenz, which armed, funded and trained a force of 480 men under Carlos Castillo Armas.

By 1954, 570,000 hectares had been redistributed to a hundred thousand families. The coup deposed Árbenz and set off decades of civil war — thirty-six years of it. Roughly two hundred thousand dead. Over a fruit company's tax declaration.

## Now bring it home

Put plainly: if you are not careful, you become a squatter in your own land. The people became labour for the company. The land was locked into growing one thing. The community got nothing and was told it was development.

Ask yourself what distinguishes that from a Zambian copper belt where the ore leaves as concentrate, or a Congolese cobalt corridor where eighty per cent of output is controlled by foreign state enterprises, or an Ivorian countryside locked into a single bean whose price is set on an exchange in London, or a Kenyan hillside growing a leaf that earns $2.28 a kilo and reaches a shelf in Hamburg at forty times that.

The differences are real: we hold the title deeds. We have flags and anthems and seats at the UN.

And the similarities are load-bearing: one crop, one buyer, terms set elsewhere, value captured elsewhere, and a political class whose position depends on the arrangement continuing.

That is not a banana republic because the fruit is different. It is a banana republic because the fruit is the only thing that is different.

## XVIII. What single rule actually costs — and the ten-times question

Now the question I have been circling, and the one everything else has been leading to: would our presidents not be richer if they stopped the bleeding?

The intuition is seductive. If you liberated the value chain, national income rises tenfold. Surely a president's share of a tenfold-larger pie beats his share of the current one? Surely corruption is just short-sightedness? Surely we could persuade them?

I spent a long time wanting this to be true. It is not, and understanding why it is not is the most important paragraph in this essay.

A rent is not a percentage of GDP. A rent is a toll on a chokepoint you personally control.

The income of an entrenched political class does not come from the size of the economy. It comes from discretion over a flow: who gets the mining licence, whose container clears the port, which firm wins the road contract, which importer receives the waiver, which bank handles the sovereign account. That income scales with opacity and discretion, not with national output.

Now apply every item on the federation list:

A supranational court whose rulings override national courts
A continental parliament with binding legislative authority
A common external tariff, removing national trade policy
A monetary authority, removing national monetary policy
A continental defence command, removing national military autonomy
Free movement, removing control over who enters and stays
Enforceable standards on elections and governance

Every single one of those is a direct attack on discretion. Harmonised rules of origin mean the customs officer cannot decide. A common tariff means the minister cannot grant the waiver. A continental court means the national court is no longer a convenience. Free movement means the permit is worthless.

Unity would make the country ten times richer and make the men currently running it far poorer — not in the long run, not eventually, but on the day the treaty enters into force.

So no. They would not accrue ten times more. They would accrue a fraction, transparently, at a salary. And we should stop constructing arguments that assume our rulers are confused. They are not confused. They have done the sum, exactly as their predecessors did in Monrovia in 1961, and they keep arriving at the same answer because it keeps being the correct answer for them.

## The incumbency landscape

Cameroon's Paul Biya has held power over forty years. Equatorial Guinea's Teodoro Obiang over forty years. Uganda's Yoweri Museveni since 1986 — nearly four decades — having overseen the removal of presidential term limits in 2005 and age limits in 2017. Rwanda's Paul Kagame, in power since 2000, oversaw a constitutional amendment permitting him to remain potentially until 2034 (Design or coincidence?—No offence intended).

And the detail that ought to be carved above the door of the AU headquarters: shortly after taking power in 1986, Museveni wrote that the problem of Africa in general, and Uganda in particular, was not the people but leaders who wanted to overstay in power (Need I repeat myself? irony — humour).

He then stayed thirty-nine years (Kettle? Pot? Black!).

I do not offer that as a cheap shot, and I want to be precise about why. It is not evidence that Museveni is a hypocrite. It is evidence that the container shapes the contents. He arrived believing what he wrote. The incentive structure of the fragmented African state converted a leader of genuine reformist conviction into a defender of the sovereignty that protects his position. That is the mechanism, in one biography.

And the AU is institutionally incapable of constraining it, for exactly the reason Nyerere named in 1963. The African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance exists. It has been widely ratified. Enforcement against a sitting head of state is essentially nonexistent. We wrote the rule and declined to build the bailiff.

## The counter-argument, given its fair hearing

There is a case on the other side, and dismissing it would make me exactly the kind of writer I do not want to be.

Scholarship examining Mugabe, Museveni and Kagame argues that indigenous African leadership systems often prioritised lineage and lifelong appointment, and that Eurocentric models emphasising fixed terms and elections were imposed by colonial administrations with little regard for existing structures — producing a durable tension between traditional practice and modern statecraft. Long-tenure leaders argue that stability and development justify continuity, and Rwanda's governance rankings are genuinely strong — eleventh of fifty-four on the Ibrahim Index, against Uganda's twenty-second, both above countries with cleaner term-limit records.

So: the cultural-legitimacy argument is real. It is also extraordinarily convenient for the people making it, and the polling does not support it. Afrobarometer's surveys across thirty-four countries and more than forty-eight thousand interviews indicate that, in principle, leaders who stay beyond two terms are not what people want.

Which means: whatever our ancestors did with chieftaincy, the living have been asked, and the living have answered.

## The hypothesis

So here is the proposition at the centre of everything I have written.

The primary obstacle to African unity is not Western interference.

Western interference is real, documented and consequential — Berlin, the franc zone, the tariff schedules, Guatemala, the Washington Agreements. I have spent twenty thousand words establishing it. But it operates through a domestic incentive structure that would resist unification even in the West's complete absence.

The people who would have to surrender power to create a United States of Africa are precisely the people who have spent their entire careers ensuring they never have to surrender power to anyone.

Nkrumah's federalism failed in 1963 because heads of state would not surrender sovereignty. It would fail today for the identical reason — with the added complication that today's leaders command patronage networks, security services and resource revenues that the class of 1963 could not have imagined.

External powers do not need to prevent African unity. They need only wait, and negotiate bilaterally in the meantime.

They are extremely good at waiting. They have had five hundred years of practice.

## XIX. Wakanda, and the thing we already have

Someone always brings up Wakanda, and I have brought it up myself, so let me deal with it and then bury it.

The fantasy is that we possessed a miracle metal, kept it, learned to build with it, and traded it on our own terms. And the irony cuts, because of course we do have the vibranium. We have cobalt, coltan, platinum, manganese, lithium, uranium, gold, and the world's second-largest rainforest sitting on a river system that could power half a continent.

But notice what the fantasy actually requires, and notice that it is not the metal.

Wakanda is not rich because it has vibranium. Wakanda is rich because it has a single sovereign authority over the entire vibranium deposit, an enforced external border, its own defence force, and no foreign concession-holders. Strip away the spaceships and Wakanda is, precisely and exactly, Nkrumah's 1961 proposal with better costumes. Continental government. Single market. African High Command. It is not a fantasy about minerals. It is a fantasy about institutions, and we rejected the institutions in a conference hall in Monrovia while the metal was already in the ground.

That is why I will not spend more time on it. The dream is not that we might one day find our vibranium. We are standing on it, and we have signed fifty-five separate contracts for it, and the dream is that we might one day stop.

## XX. Then what? Four roads, in descending order of comfort

If the maximalist version is blocked — and I have just spent an entire section arguing that it is blocked by design — what remains?

## Path One: Functional integration without political union

Make AfCFTA real. Enforce SAATM. Harmonise rules of origin so regional mineral value chains can form. Build the corridors. Leave sovereignty formally untouched while making the economics of separation progressively more expensive.

This is the current strategy. Its ceiling is limited — the World Bank projects AfCFTA implementation could cut intra-African trade costs by 16%, with full implementation raising Africa's GDP by around 10% by 2043 — but its floor is safe, because it never requires a president to surrender anything he cares about.

The critique writes itself: it is precisely because it threatens nothing that it changes little. Signature without compliance is the pattern. Eight thousand five hundred certificates of origin is the pattern. SAATM is the pattern.

## Path Two: Regional blocs first, federation later

Let the regional economic communities lead. The EAC and SADC already have real economic and political cooperation and could liberalise deeply within their regions before anyone attempts fifty-four at once. This is the EU's actual historical model: start small, among states of comparable interest, deepen, then widen.

The critique: ECOWAS is fraying, not deepening. Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger withdrew in 2024. Regional blocs are not obviously more stable than the continental project, and the EU analogy flatters us — six states of comparable wealth is not fifty-four with five colonial languages, forty currencies and debt profiles ranging from investment-grade to default.

## Path Three: Federation under external pressure

The historical pattern for genuine political union is that it follows catastrophe or acute existential threat. America federated properly only after a civil war. Europe integrated from the ashes of 1945 — not from romantic pan-European sentiment, of which there was none, but from exhaustion and terror.

Africa's plausible forcing function is the resource competition now accelerating. If the continent watches its lithium, cobalt and rare earths extracted bilaterally at five per cent of value while conflict escalates in the Kivus, the case for coordinated negotiation becomes harder for even entrenched incumbents to dismiss — not on moral grounds, but on revenue grounds.

The cynical version of the optimistic case: African leaders will federate when fragmentation costs them personally more than unity does. Not before.

## Path Four: the one nobody writes about, which is you

Every path above is addressed to heads of state. Which is why every path above has failed for sixty-three years. We keep writing petitions to the beneficiaries of the problem.

So let me propose the fourth road, and it is the only one that does not require asking permission from the people who have already answered.

The gap that matters is not the signature gap. It is the enforcement gap — and enforcement gaps close under observation.

Concretely:

Publish the compliance league table. Not ratifications — ratifications are theatre. Publish, quarterly and by name, which states have gazetted their tariff schedules, which have filed complete Category A/B/C offers, which have issued certificates of origin and how many, and which SAATM signatories have denied traffic rights to which carriers. Twenty-five countries are operational. Name the other twenty-nine. Every week.

Make the non-tariff barrier reportable and public. A trader blocked at Malaba or Beitbridge should be able to file, publicly, in an hour. Aggregate it. Rank the borders.

Demand a beneficiation floor in every new mineral contract. Zimbabwe's ban produced a $400 million refinery. The instrument works. It is not a theory.

Ask your MP a single question and do not accept an answer about aspiration: Has our country gazetted its AfCFTA schedules? Yes or no? If no, why not, and when?

Treat the COPEC lesson as policy, not history. Two producers cannot hold a floor price. A continental commodity authority for cocoa, cobalt, copper, coffee and platinum can. Ask why the AU has never attempted it. The answer will tell you who it is for.

Because here is the thing about the sovereignty shield: it works against courts, against treaties, against other heads of state. It has no defence at all against being watched by your own citizens, in numbers, continuously, with specific questions and public scorecards.

That is not a revolution with a gun. That is a revolution with a spreadsheet. And the spreadsheet is the only one of the two that has never once put a Compaoré in power.

## XXI. The map, and the size of us

I want to end where my curiosity paused, on something that sounds small and is not.

Even the drawing of us is shrunk. The Mercator projection, created in 1569 for navigation, preserves shape and destroys size — inflating everything near the poles and compressing everything near the equator. On Mercator, Greenland and Africa appear roughly the same size. In reality, fourteen Greenlands fit inside Africa. Africa's land area exceeds 30 million square kilometres.

Every classroom on this continent hangs a map that makes us small. We have been looking at a diminished version of ourselves for four hundred years, in geography lessons, on news broadcasts, in the corner of every weather report, and we have called it a map.

As I wrote this I questioned whether our education systems are built to keep us inside an illusion. I will not indulge the full conspiracy — most of your teachers are not agents of anything; they are overworked people using the textbooks they were given. But a curriculum does not need an author to have an effect. If a child spends twelve years looking at a projection that shrinks her continent, learning a history that begins at contact, and taking an examination that never once asks her what raw cobalt costs against refined cobalt, she will emerge fluent, credentialed, and structurally unable to see the thing.

That is not a plot. That is inertia, which is more durable than any plot, because nobody has to maintain it.

And then, this month, something happened.

The African Union backed the Correct the Map campaign, and the United Nations passed a resolution — 164 votes in favour — encouraging wider use of equal-area projections such as Equal Earth in classrooms, media and international institutions, so that the world map finally reflects Africa's true scale. Carlos Lopes, one of the sharpest analytical voices on African economic strategy, called it an emotional day.

And I am glad. I am not being sardonic. Representation is real, and a child who sees the true size of her home carries something she would not otherwise have.

But I want us to hold both facts in one hand, because holding only one is how sixty-three years disappear.

In September 2026, one hundred and sixty-four nations voted to acknowledge that Africa is bigger than they had been drawing it.

And in September 2026, a Kenyan still cannot fly to Lagos without paying sixty per cent more than the equivalent European route, in taxes that frequently exceed the fare itself. Twenty-nine African states have not gazetted the schedules that would let their traders use the free trade area they ratified. Eight thousand five hundred and sixty-one certificates of origin have been issued for a market of 1.4 billion people. The cobalt is leaving at ten dollars a kilo. The tea is leaving at $2.28. The bean is leaving raw, and Germany — which cannot grow a single one — out-earns the entire continent that gave the world coffee.

We won the map. We have not yet won the kilogram.

## XXII. The honest conclusion

The romantic case for African unity is Nkrumah's: that we are one people, artificially divided, and that reunification is a restoration.

The realist case is colder and, I think, more useful.

Fragmentation is not primarily a wound to be healed. It is a business model to be dismantled.

It benefits external powers who negotiate bilaterally and price accordingly. It benefits domestic elites whose power depends on the sovereign container and the discretion it confers. It benefits intermediary states running smuggling economies that exist only because borders are simultaneously arbitrary and enforced. It benefits the roaster in Hamburg, the refiner in Zhejiang, the grinder in Amsterdam, the assayer in London, and roughly four hundred men on this continent with residences in three countries.

Every one of those beneficiaries has a more immediate incentive to preserve the arrangement than any diffuse population has to change it.

That is why sixty-three years of pan-African rhetoric has produced a free trade agreement most members have not operationalised and an air transport market its own signatories decline to honour.

Nkrumah said: we unite or we perish. The continent found a third option he did not anticipate. Neither unite nor perish, but persist — fragmented, individually negotiating, collectively underpriced, and always, always about to integrate next year.

So let me close by addressing the two audiences this was written for, because they require different sentences.

## To the presidents

You are not confused. I have stopped pretending you are, and I would ask you to stop pretending too. You have run the numbers, exactly as Houphouët-Boigny ran them in Monrovia in 1961, and you have concluded that a smaller kingdom fully held is worth more than a larger one shared.

You are right about your own position and wrong about its duration. The arrangement that protects you is not stable. It is merely slow. Ask Compaoré, who held it twenty-seven years and now hears his conviction read in absentia. Ask the men who thought the CFA was permanent, and then watched three of their neighbours walk out and start printing. Ask any head of state on this continent under the age of sixty what the median citizen's age is, and whether that citizen — who is nineteen, unemployed, on a phone containing Congolese cobalt she will never be paid for — is going to spend her forties asking politely.

Sovereignty, the thing you are protecting, was handed to you in 1963 as a shield. It was never a sword. It has never once been used to get a better price for anything your people grow or dig.

Sign the schedules. Open the skies. Harmonise the codes. Not because it is noble. Because the alternative is to be the last generation of men who could have done it, and everyone will know your names.

## And to everyone else

We have been told the obstacle is Europe, and it is partly Europe. We have been told the obstacle is China, and it is partly China. These are comfortable enemies, because they are far away and nothing is required of us but anger.

The nearer obstacle is a class of men who look like us, speak our languages, were educated in our schools, and have arrived — rationally, repeatedly, over three generations — at the conclusion that our fragmentation is worth more to them than our unity.

That is harder to say at a funeral or on a podcast. It is also actionable, which the other version is not.

They vote against unity in every forum they enter, and they will keep doing it until the price of voting that way exceeds the price of voting the other way. You are the only mechanism on earth that can raise that price. Not a court they can ignore. Not a charter they can ratify and shelve. Not a foreign power that profits from their weakness.

You. Watching. Counting. Naming. Refusing to accept a communiqué in place of a customs gazette.

Sixty-three years ago, twenty-two of twenty-seven men decided that their comfort outweighed our arithmetic, and we have paid for that meeting every single day since — in a cup of tea that earns a Kenyan grandmother half a cent, in a kilogram of cobalt that leaves Kolwezi at ten dollars and returns at two hundred, in a flight to Lagos that costs more in tax than in fare.

The question for this generation is not whether Nkrumah was right. He obviously was.

The question is whether anything short of catastrophe can make his argument politically survivable for the people who would have to act on it.

And the only honest answer I have — the one that keeps me writing at this hour — is that catastrophe and attention are the only two forces that have ever moved a ruling class, and exactly one of them is available to us before it arrives.

Choose the spreadsheet. Choose it loudly. Choose it now.

Because the borders were drawn to limit us. The word has been sitting there, in plain sight, since 1884.

Everything they intended was written down. We just never read it aloud.
